Statement: $\sqrt{2}$ cannot be written as a ratio of two integers.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Preface.lyx: irrationality of sqrt(2).

Statement: In a right triangle, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Working-in-Rn, Pythagoras in inner product spaces. Linear Algebra 2: §5.4.3 orthogonality; the card is the classical Euclidean case.

Statement: $\displaystyle 1 + \frac12 + \frac13 + \frac14 + \cdots$ grows without bound.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - series.lyx: harmonic series.

Statement: $\displaystyle \frac{\pi}{4} = 1 - \frac13 + \frac15 - \frac17 + \cdots$
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - taylor.lyx: Taylor series of arctan, endpoint pi/4.

Statement: $(a + b)^n$ expands with the binomial coefficients of Pascal's triangle.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Preface.lyx: binomial formula. Mathematical topic matches; Pascal/1665 attribution requires review.

Statement: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, then $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ satisfies $F'(x)=f(x)$ for $a<x<b$.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-Riemann_int-reviewed.lyx: fundamental theorem / Newton–Leibniz.

Statement: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)$ with $a<b$, then $f'(c)=0$ for some $c\in(a,b)$.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - derivative.lyx: Rolle.

Statement: Suppose $f,g$ are differentiable on $(a,b)$, $g'$ never vanishes, and $f(x),g(x)\to0$ as $x\to a^+$. If $f'(x)/g'(x)\to L$, then $f(x)/g(x)\to L$ (also for infinite $L$).
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - derivative.lyx: L’Hôpital, including one-sided 0/0 limits.

Statement: For $f\in C^{n+1}$ on an interval containing $a$ and $x$, $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k+\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}$ for some $c$ between $a$ and $x$.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - taylor.lyx: Taylor with Lagrange remainder.

Statement: As $n\to\infty$, $\displaystyle\frac{n!}{\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n}\to1$.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-improper_int-reviewed.lyx: Stirling.

Statement: $\displaystyle 1 + \frac14 + \frac19 + \frac1{16} + \cdots = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-fourier-reviewed.lyx: evaluation of the sum of reciprocal squares.

Statement: $e$ is irrational.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - taylor.lyx: cor:e is irrational-1.

Statement: $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$, and in particular $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$.
Course evidence: Calc 2: Fourier series and complex exponentials. ODE lesson4.tex: complex eigenvalues and exponentials.

Statement: A square linear system with nonzero determinant is solved by ratios of determinants.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 1: §3.9, Theorem 186, Cramer’s rule, printed p. 48.

Statement:
Let $f,g$ be $C^1$ near $p$. If $f$ has a local extremum at $p$ subject to $g=0$, and $
abla g(p)
e0$, then $
abla f(p)=\lambda
abla g(p)$ for some real $\lambda$.
Course evidence: Calc 3 / Chapter-Fundamental-thms-reviewed.lyx: Lagrange multipliers; published chapter 3.

Statement: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, with $a<b$, then $f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ for some $c\in(a,b)$.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - derivative.lyx: Lagrange mean value theorem.

Statement: Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a root in $\mathbb C$.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 2: §7.4, fundamental theorem of algebra; used for eigenvalues over C.

Statement: For a Riemann-integrable function $f$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$, with $\hat f(n)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)e^{-inx}\,dx$, $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}|\hat f(n)|^2=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|f(x)|^2\,dx$.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-fourier-reviewed.lyx: Parseval for Riemann-integrable functions.

Statement: Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.
Course evidence: Calc 1: sequences, Bolzano–Weierstrass. Calc 2: compactness. Calc 3: continuity in Rn, bounded subsequences. ODE lesson3.tex: explicitly used in Arzelà–Ascoli proof.

Statement: A continuous function on $[a, b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - Functions and continuity.lyx: intermediate value theorem.

Statement: The radius of convergence of $\sum a_n x^n$ is $1 \big/ \limsup |a_n|^{1/n}$.
Course evidence: Calc 1: series, Cauchy–Hadamard radius. Calc 2: power-series, radius of convergence. This card already existed; no duplicate added.

Statement: In an inner product space, $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$ for all vectors $u,v$.
Course evidence: Calc 2: metric/vector-function chapters. Calc 3: Working-in-Rn, inner products. Linear Algebra 2: §5.4.2, Cauchy–Schwarz.

Statement: If $f,g$ are continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, with $a<b$, some $c\in(a,b)$ satisfies $(f(b)-f(a))g'(c)=(g(b)-g(a))f'(c)$.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - derivative.lyx: Cauchy mean value theorem.

Statement: If $\sum a_n$ converges, then $\sum a_n x^n \to \sum a_n$ as $x \to 1^-$.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-power-series-reviewed.lyx: Abel at the endpoint. Calc 1’s Abel radius theorem is a different result.

Statement: The Fourier series of a piecewise smooth periodic function converges to it (to the average at jumps).
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-fourier-reviewed.lyx: pointwise convergence of Fourier series.

Statement: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 2: §6.1, self-adjoint maps; real symmetric case.

Statement: For a real symmetric matrix $A$ and any invertible real matrix $P$, the matrices $A$ and $P^TAP$ have the same numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 2: §5.3, quadratic forms and inertia.

Statement: A conditionally convergent series of real numbers can be rearranged to sum to any prescribed real number.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - series.lyx: rearrangements of conditionally convergent real series.

Statement: Every complex square matrix is similar to a block-diagonal matrix of Jordan blocks.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 2: chapter 4, Jordan form. ODE lesson4.tex: Jordan canonical form explicitly recalled and used for linear systems.

Statement: There is a function continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-function-series-reviewed.lyx: construction of a continuous nowhere differentiable function. Calc 1 only previews it.

Statement: A continuous function on a closed bounded interval is uniformly continuous.
Course evidence: Calc 1: functions/continuity, uniform continuity. Calc 2: compactness. Calc 3: Continuity-in-Rn, Heine–Cantor; card states the interval case.

Statement: The number $e$ is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-Riemann_int-reviewed.lyx: transcendence of e, Hermite argument.

Statement: Every derivative has the intermediate value property, even if it is not continuous.
Course evidence: Calc 1 / Chapter - derivative.lyx: Darboux on derivatives.

Statement: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 2: chapter 2, Cayley–Hamilton with proof.

Statement: A pointwise monotone sequence of continuous real-valued functions on a compact space, converging pointwise to a continuous function, converges uniformly.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-function-series-reviewed.lyx: Dini.

Statement: Every continuous function on $[a, b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-function-series-reviewed.lyx: Weierstrass polynomial approximation.

Statement: A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-compactness-reviewed.lyx: compactness in Euclidean space. Calc 3 / Chapter-Working-in-Rn-reviewed.lyx: compact subsets of Rn.

Statement: For a continuous periodic function, the arithmetic means of the first $N$ Fourier partial sums converge uniformly to the function as $N\to\infty$.
Course evidence: Calc 2 / Chapter-fourier-reviewed.lyx: Fejér.

Statement: A bounded function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable exactly when its discontinuities have measure zero.
Course evidence: Calc 2: Riemann_int, criterion discussed without proof. Calc 3: Integration-in-Rn, Lebesgue criterion with proof; all integration chapters included.

Statement: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]\times[c,d]$, then $\displaystyle\int_a^b\!\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx=\int_c^d\!\int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx\,dy=\iint_{[a,b]\times[c,d]}f$.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Integration-in-Rn, Fubini. Card narrowed to continuous functions on a rectangle, a direct instance of the course theorem.

Statement: Every continuous map from a closed disk (or ball) to itself has a fixed point.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Integration-in-Rn, a variation on Brouwer (enrichment); includes a related fixed-point formulation.

Statement: If $X$ is a nonempty complete metric space and $T:X\to X$ satisfies $d(Tx,Ty)\le qd(x,y)$ for a fixed $0\le q<1$, then $T$ has a unique fixed point.
Course evidence: Calc 2: complete-metric-spaces, contraction theorem. ODE lesson3.tex: Contractions and existence/uniqueness via fixed points.

Statement: Every bounded monotone sequence of real numbers converges to a real limit.
Course evidence: Calc 1: Chapter - sequences and limits.lyx, bounded monotone sequences.
Historical source: Dedekind, Stetigkeit und irrationale Zahlen (1872), §7: https://doi.org/10.3931/e-rara-71757

Statement: A real sequence $(a_n)$ converges iff, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is $N$ such that $|a_m-a_n|<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$.
Course evidence: Calc 1: sequences and limits, Cauchy sequences. Calc 2: complete metric spaces, completeness of R.
Historical source: Cauchy, Cours d’analyse (1821), original text: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Cours_d’analyse_de_l’École_royale_polytechnique/Texte_entier

Statement: If $I_1\supseteq I_2\supseteq\cdots$ are nonempty closed bounded intervals in $\mathbb R$, their intersection is nonempty. If their lengths tend to zero, it consists of one point.
Course evidence: Calc 1: sequences and limits, Cantor’s nested-interval lemma.
Historical source: Cantor, Ueber eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffes aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen (1874): https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1874.77.258

Statement: If $a_n\to L$, then $\displaystyle\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\to L$.
Course evidence: Calc 1: sequences and limits, Cesàro means.
Historical source: Cauchy, Cours d’analyse (1821), original text: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Cours_d’analyse_de_l’École_royale_polytechnique/Texte_entier

Statement: If $b_n$ is strictly increasing to $+\infty$ and $\displaystyle\frac{a_{n+1}-a_n}{b_{n+1}-b_n}\to L\in\mathbb R$, then $a_n/b_n\to L$.
Course evidence: Calc 1: sequences and limits, Stolz theorem.
Historical source: Stolz, Vorlesungen über allgemeine Arithmetik I (1885), pp. 173–175: https://archive.org/details/vorlesungenber01stoluoft

Statement: If $a_n\ge0$ decreases to zero, then $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}a_n$ converges, with error after $N$ terms at most $a_{N+1}$.
Course evidence: Calc 1: Chapter - series.lyx, Leibniz test.
Historical source: Leibniz to Johann Bernoulli, 25 October 1713; correspondence chronology: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/OfTheDay/oftheday-10-25/

Statement: For an eventually nonzero sequence, let $L=\lim |a_{n+1}/a_n|$. The series $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely if $L<1$ and diverges if $L>1$. The case $L=1$ is inconclusive.
Course evidence: Calc 1: series, ratio test. Calc 2: power-series radius examples.
Historical source: d’Alembert, Réflexions sur les suites divergentes ou convergentes, Opuscules mathématiques V (1768), pp. 171–183: https://www.exhibit.xavier.edu/oresme_2017Sept/3/

Statement: Let $L=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n}$. Then $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely if $L<1$ and diverges if $L>1$; $L=1$ is inconclusive.
Course evidence: Calc 1: series, root test. Calc 2: power series.
Historical source: Cauchy, Cours d’analyse (1821), original text: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Cours_d’analyse_de_l’École_royale_polytechnique/Texte_entier

Statement: If the partial sums of $\sum a_n$ are bounded and the real sequence $b_n$ decreases to zero, then $\sum a_nb_n$ converges.
Course evidence: Calc 1: series, Dirichlet test. Calc 2: function-series tests.
Historical source: Dirichlet, Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie, edited by Dedekind (1863), §101: https://archive.org/details/vorlesungenberz01dirigoog

Statement: If $\sum a_n$ converges and $(b_n)$ is a bounded monotone real sequence, then $\sum a_nb_n$ converges.
Course evidence: Calc 1: series, Abel test. Calc 2: function-series tests.
Historical source: Abel, Untersuchungen über die Reihe …, J. reine angew. Math. 1 (1826), §2, theorem 3: https://geodesic.mathdoc.fr/volume/JRAM_1826__1/

Statement: A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact set attains its maximum and minimum. In particular, this holds on a closed bounded interval.
Course evidence: Calc 1: functions and continuity, Weierstrass theorem. Calc 2: compactness. Calc 3: continuity in Rn.
Historical source: Weierstrass’s 1861 lectures; historical timeline in Differential Calculus: From Practice to Theory: https://roam.libraries.psu.edu/system/files/e-books/MATH-Differential_Calculus_From_Practice_to_Theory.pdf

Statement: If $f$ is differentiable at an interior point $x_0$ of its domain and has a local maximum or minimum there, then $f'(x_0)=0$.
Course evidence: Calc 1: derivative, Fermat theorem. Calc 3: extrema via directional derivatives.
Historical source: Fermat, Methodus ad disquirendam maximam et minimam, in Varia opera mathematica (1679); source text in Stedall, Mathematics Emerging, §3.1.1.

Statement: If $f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $g$ at $f(x)$, then $(g\circ f)'(x)=g'(f(x))f'(x)$. For differentiable maps between Euclidean spaces, $D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))Df(x)$.
Course evidence: Calc 1: derivative, chain rule. Calc 3: Diff-in-Rn, chain rule.
Historical source: Lagrange, Théorie des fonctions analytiques (1797), §31; historical research: https://scholarworks.umt.edu/tme/vol7/iss2/10/

Statement: A bounded function $f$ on a closed interval is Riemann integrable iff, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some partition $P$ satisfies $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$.
Course evidence: Calc 2: Riemann_int, upper/lower sums. Calc 3: Integration-in-Rn, box analogue.
Historical source: Darboux, Mémoire sur les fonctions discontinues (1875): https://doi.org/10.24033/asens.122

Statement: If continuous functions $f_n:X\to\mathbb R$ on a metric space converge uniformly to $f$, then $f$ is continuous.
Course evidence: Calc 2: function-series, uniform limits and continuity.
Historical source: Viertel (2021), historical research on Weierstrass lecture manuscripts: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00407-020-00266-9

Statement: If $|f_n(x)|\le M_n$ for every $x\in X$, with $M_n\ge0$ and $\sum M_n<\infty$, then $\sum f_n$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $X$.
Course evidence: Calc 2: function-series, Weierstrass majorant test.
Historical source: Viertel (2021), historical research on Weierstrass lecture manuscripts: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00407-020-00266-9

Statement: If Riemann-integrable $f_n$ converge uniformly to $f$ on $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Riemann integrable and $\displaystyle\int_a^b f=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n$.
Course evidence: Calc 2: function-series, exchange of limit and integral.
Historical source: Viertel (2021), historical research on Weierstrass lecture manuscripts: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00407-020-00266-9

Statement: Let $f_n\in C^1([a,b])$. If $\sum f_n(x_0)$ converges at one point and $\sum f_n'$ converges uniformly, then $f=\sum f_n$ converges uniformly and $f'=\sum f_n'$.
Course evidence: Calc 2: function-series, differentiation and limits.
Historical source: Viertel (2021), historical research on Weierstrass lecture manuscripts: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00407-020-00266-9

Statement: If $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$, then $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\cos(\lambda x)\,dx\to0$ and $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\sin(\lambda x)\,dx\to0$ as $\lambda\to+\infty$.
Course evidence: Calc 2: fourier, Riemann–Lebesgue lemma.
Historical source: Riemann, Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe (written 1854, published 1867); original-paper history: https://www.cfm.brown.edu/people/dobrush/am36/Mathematica/ch2/fourier.html

Topics: Continuity and compactness;Function sequences and series;ODE existence and uniqueness
Statement: Every uniformly bounded, equicontinuous sequence of real continuous functions on $[a,b]$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence.
Course evidence: Calc 2: compactness, Arzelà–Ascoli. ODE: lesson3.tex, Peano proof via equicontinuity.
Historical source: Arzelà, Sulle funzioni di linee (1895); original-work bibliography: https://www.numdam.org/item/MSM_1930__44__1_0/

Statement: If $F:U\subset\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ is $C^1$ on an open set and $DF(a)$ is invertible, then $F$ has a $C^1$ inverse near $a$, with $D(F^{-1})(F(a))=DF(a)^{-1}$.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Fundamental-thms, inverse function theorem.
Historical source: Dontchev and Rockafellar, Implicit Functions and Solution Mappings, historical commentary, p. 57: https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf

Statement: Let $F:U\subset\mathbb R^{n+m}\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ on an open set, with $F(a,b)=0$ and invertible $D_yF(a,b)$. Near $(a,b)$ the zero set is exactly $y=g(x)$ for a unique $C^1$ function $g$ with $g(a)=b$.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Fundamental-thms, implicit function theorem.
Historical source: Dontchev and Rockafellar, Implicit Functions and Solution Mappings, historical commentary, p. 57: https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf

Statement: If $f\in C^2(U)$ on an open set $U\subset\mathbb R^n$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for all $i,j$.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Diff-in-Rn, equality of mixed second derivatives.
Historical source: Schwarz, Communication, Archives des sciences physiques et naturelles 48 (1873), 38–45; collected works: https://archive.org/details/gesammeltemathem02schwuoft

Theorem: Change of variables in multiple integrals
Statement: Let $\Phi:U\to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $A\subset U$ compact and Jordan measurable, and $f$ continuous on $\Phi(A)$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{\Phi(A)}f(y)\,dy=\int_A f(\Phi(x))|\det D\Phi(x)|\,dx$.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Integration-in-Rn, change of variables and Jacobian.
Historical source: Jacobi, De determinantibus functionalibus (1841), J. reine angew. Math. 22: https://www.degruyterbrill.com/journal/key/crll/1841/22/html

Statement: For $s>0$, define $\displaystyle\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$. Then $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$ and $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$ for every integer $n\ge0$.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Improper Integration in Rn, Gamma function.
Historical source: Euler E19, De progressionibus transcendentibus … (written 1729, published 1738): https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/euler-works/19/

Statement: $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$
Course evidence: Calc 3: Improper Integration in Rn, Gaussian integral and polar coordinates.
Historical source: Laplace, Mémoire sur la probabilité des causes par les événements (1774); original-source extracts: https://www.york.ac.uk/depts/maths/histstat/normal_history.pdf

Statement: For convex bodies $K,L\subset\mathbb R^n$, $\displaystyle |K+L|^{1/n}\ge |K|^{1/n}+|L|^{1/n}$, where $|\cdot|$ is volume and $K+L=\{x+y:x\in K,y\in L\}$.
Course evidence: Calc 3: Integration-in-Rn, Brunn–Minkowski enrichment section.
Historical source: Minkowski, Geometrie der Zahlen (1896); original research survey with historical references: https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-02-00941-2

Statement: If $F(t,x)$ is continuous near $(t_0,x_0)$ and locally Lipschitz in $x$ uniformly in $t$, then $x'=F(t,x)$, $x(t_0)=x_0$, has a unique local solution.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson3.tex, Existence and Uniqueness theorem and Picard iterations.
Historical source: Picard, Sur le théorème général relatif à l’existence des intégrales … (1891): https://www.numdam.org/item/NAM_1891_3_10__197_0/

Statement: If $F(t,x)$ is continuous near $(t_0,x_0)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, then $x'=F(t,x)$, $x(t_0)=x_0$, has at least one local solution. Uniqueness need not hold.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson3.tex, Peano’s theorem.
Historical source: Peano, Démonstration de l’intégrabilité des équations différentielles ordinaires, Math. Ann. 37 (1890), 182–228; original text: https://www.mathematik.uni-marburg.de/~eckert/2003SS/Blatt00bis13.pdf

Statement: If $u,b\ge0$ are continuous on $[a,T]$, $A\ge0$, and $\displaystyle u(t)\le A+\int_a^t b(s)u(s)\,ds$, then $\displaystyle u(t)\le A\exp\!\left(\int_a^t b(s)\,ds\right)$.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson3.tex, Gronwall’s Inequality and dependence on parameters.
Historical source: Grönwall, Note on the Derivatives with Respect to a Parameter …, Ann. Math. 20 (1919), 292–296: https://doi.org/10.2307/1967124

Statement: For continuous $F$, suppose $|F(t,x)-F(t,y)|\le\omega(|x-y|)$ locally, where $\omega$ is continuous, nondecreasing, positive for $r>0$, and $\omega(0)=0$. If $\int_{0^+}dr/\omega(r)=\infty$, the initial-value problem has local uniqueness.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson3.tex, Osgood’s condition.
Historical source: Osgood, Beweis der Existenz einer Lösung … ohne Hinzunahme der Cauchy-Lipschitz’schen Bedingung (1898): https://zenodo.org/records/2150462

Statement: If $A(t)$ is a continuous matrix and $X'(t)=A(t)X(t)$, then $\displaystyle\det X(t)=\det X(t_0)\exp\!\left(\int_{t_0}^{t}\operatorname{tr}A(s)\,ds\right)$.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson4.tex, Linear non-autonomous / The Wronskian.
Historical source: Liouville, Note sur la Théorie des Équations différentielles (1838): https://www.numdam.org/item/JMPA_1838_1_3__255_0/

Statement:
For $x'=F(x)$ with $F\in C^1$ and $F(0)=0$, suppose a $C^1$ function $V$ near $0$ satisfies $V(0)=0$, $V(x)>0$ for $x
e0$, and $
abla V(x)\cdot F(x)\le0$. Then $0$ is stable; strict negativity for $x
e0$ gives asymptotic stability.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson5.tex, The Liapounov stability method.
Historical source: Lyapunov, The General Problem of the Stability of Motion (1892); original memoir discussed and the method developed in LaSalle (1960): https://www.et.byu.edu/~beard/papers/library/LaSalle60a.pdf

Topics: Stability and phase portraits;Linear ODE systems
Statement: For $x'=F(x)$ with $F\in C^1$ and $F(0)=0$, if every eigenvalue of $DF(0)$ has negative real part, then $0$ is locally asymptotically stable.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson5.tex, Linearization / A non-linear sink.
Historical source: Lyapunov, The General Problem of the Stability of Motion (1892); original memoir discussed and the method developed in LaSalle (1960): https://www.et.byu.edu/~beard/papers/library/LaSalle60a.pdf

Statement: Let $K$ be compact and positively invariant for a $C^1$ autonomous system, and let $V\in C^1$ near $K$ satisfy $\dot V\le0$ on $K$. Every trajectory starting in $K$ approaches the largest invariant subset of $\{x\in K:\dot V(x)=0\}$.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson5.tex, Lasalle’s invariance principle.
Historical source: LaSalle, Some Extensions of Liapunov’s Second Method (1960): https://doi.org/10.1109/TCT.1960.1086720

Statement: For a $C^1$ planar autonomous system, if a forward trajectory stays in a compact subset of the domain and its $\omega$-limit set contains no equilibrium, that limit set is a periodic orbit.
Course evidence: ODE: lesson7.tex, Poincaré–Bendixson formulation and proof.
Historical source: Bendixson, Sur les courbes définies par des équations différentielles, Acta Math. 24 (1901), 1–88: https://archive.ymsc.tsinghua.edu.cn/pacm_download/117/5067-11511_2006_Article_BF02403068.pdf

Statement: For finite-dimensional subspaces $U,W$ of a vector space, $\dim(U+W)+\dim(U\cap W)=\dim U+\dim W$.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 1: Corollary 103, printed pp. 29–30. Linear Algebra 2: eigenspace sums, chapter 1.
Historical source: Grassmann, Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre (1844), original book: https://www.e-rara.ch/zut/content/titleinfo/1169335

Statement: If $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ are linearly independent and $w_1,\ldots,w_n$ span the same ambient vector space, then $m\le n$ and $m$ of the $w_j$ can be replaced by the $v_i$ while preserving spanning.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 1: §2.10, basis and dimension.
Historical source: Grassmann, Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre (1844), original book: https://www.e-rara.ch/zut/content/titleinfo/1169335

Statement: If $T:V\to W$ is linear and $V$ is finite dimensional, then $\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim V$.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 1: Theorem 101, printed p. 29. Linear Algebra 2: kernel/eigenspace dimension arguments.
Historical source: Sylvester, Lectures on the Principles of Universal Algebra (1884), definition of nullity; collected works IV: https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/sylvester4.pdf

Statement: For square matrices $A,B$ of the same size over a field, $\det(AB)=\det A\,\det B$.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 1: Theorem 171, printed p. 43. Linear Algebra 2: characteristic polynomial under similarity.
Historical source: Cauchy, Mémoire sur les fonctions qui ne peuvent obtenir que deux valeurs égales et de signes contraires … (1815); original-source teaching project: https://old.maa.org/node/137453

Statement: For any $n\times n$ matrix $A=(a_{ij})$ and any row $i$, $\displaystyle\det A=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(-1)^{i+j}a_{ij}\det A_{ij}$, where $A_{ij}$ deletes row $i$ and column $j$.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 1: Proposition 177, printed p. 45.
Historical source: Laplace, Recherches sur le calcul intégral et sur le système du monde, Mémoires de l’Académie royale des sciences, année 1772 (published 1776); original memoir reprinted in Œuvres complètes VIII.

Statement: Every linearly independent list $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ in an inner product space admits an orthonormal list $e_1,\ldots,e_k$ with $\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_j)=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\ldots,v_j)$ for each $j$.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 2: §5.4.3, orthogonality and orthonormal bases.
Historical source: Schmidt, Zur Theorie der linearen und nichtlinearen Integralgleichungen I (1907): https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01449770 ; historical research: https://doi.org/10.1002/nla.1839

Statement: In a finite-dimensional real inner product space, every linear functional $\ell$ has a unique representing vector $u$ such that $\ell(v)=\langle v,u\rangle$ for all $v$.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 2: §6.4.1, Riesz theorem as needed in the course.
Historical source: Riesz, Sur une espèce de géométrie analytique des systèmes de fonctions sommables, C. R. Acad. Sci. 144 (1907), 1409–1411; Fréchet, same volume, 1414–1416. Original-work references: https://numdam.org/articles/10.24033/rhm.57/

Statement: A complex square matrix $A$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors iff $A^*A=AA^*$. Equivalently, a normal matrix is unitarily diagonalizable.
Course evidence: Linear Algebra 2: Theorem 6.4.16, printed p. 136.
Historical source: Schur, Über die charakteristischen Wurzeln einer linearen Substitution … (1909): https://www.digizeitschriften.de/download/pdf/235181684_0066/log49.pdf
